#### Transformations to Improve Fit and Equalize Variances {#sec-pmd-624}

[**Transformations**]{#sec-pmd-624-transformations}

In regression modeling, we often apply transformations to achieve the following two goals:

1. to satisfy the homogeneity of variances assumption for the errors.
2. to linearize the fit as much as possible.

Some care and judgment is required in that these two goals can conflict. We generally try to achieve homogeneous variances first and then address the issue of trying to linearize the fit.

[**Plot of Common Transformations to Obtain Homogeneous Variances**]{#sec-pmd-624-ytransform}

The first step is to try transforming the response variable to find a transformation that will equalize the variances. In practice, the square root, ln, and reciprocal transformations often work well for this purpose. We will try these first.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| message: false
#| label: fig-pmd-624-response-transformations
#| fig-cap: "Field defect size versus lab defect size in its original units and transformed by square root, natural log, and reciprocal"
library(patchwork)

berger <- read_table(
  here::here("datasets", "BERGER1.DAT"),
  skip = 25,
  col_names = c("field", "lab", "batch"),
  col_types = "ddi"
)

p_orig <- ggplot(berger, aes(lab, field)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Lab Defect Size", y = "Field Defect Size") +
  theme_light()

p_sqrt <- ggplot(berger, aes(lab, sqrt(field))) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Lab Defect Size", y = "sqrt(Field Defect Size)") +
  theme_light()

p_ln <- ggplot(berger, aes(lab, log(field))) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Lab Defect Size", y = "ln(Field Defect Size)") +
  theme_light()

p_inv <- ggplot(berger, aes(lab, 1 / field)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Lab Defect Size", y = "1 / Field Defect Size") +
  theme_light()

(p_orig + p_sqrt) / (p_ln + p_inv)
```

In examining these plots, we are looking for the plot that shows the most constant variability across the horizontal range of the plot.

This plot indicates that the ln transformation is a good candidate model for achieving the most homogeneous variances.

[**Plot of Common Transformations to Linearize the Fit**]{#sec-pmd-624-xtransform}

One problem with applying the above transformation is that the plot indicates that a straight-line fit will no longer be an adequate model for the data. We address this problem by attempting to find a transformation of the predictor variable that will result in the most linear fit. In practice, the square root, ln, and reciprocal transformations often work well for this purpose. We will try these first.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-pmd-624-predictor-transformations
#| fig-cap: "ln(Field defect size) versus lab defect size in its original units and transformed by square root, natural log, and reciprocal"
p_lnf_orig <- ggplot(berger, aes(lab, log(field))) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Lab Defect Size", y = "ln(Field Defect Size)") +
  theme_light()

p_lnf_sqrt <- ggplot(berger, aes(sqrt(lab), log(field))) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "sqrt(Lab Defect Size)", y = "ln(Field Defect Size)") +
  theme_light()

p_lnf_ln <- ggplot(berger, aes(log(lab), log(field))) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "ln(Lab Defect Size)", y = "ln(Field Defect Size)") +
  theme_light()

p_lnf_inv <- ggplot(berger, aes(1 / lab, log(field))) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "1 / Lab Defect Size", y = "ln(Field Defect Size)") +
  theme_light()

(p_lnf_orig + p_lnf_sqrt) / (p_lnf_ln + p_lnf_inv)
```

This plot shows that the ln transformation of the predictor variable is a good candidate model.

[**Box-Cox Linearity Plot**]{#sec-pmd-624-boxcox}

The previous step can be approached more formally by the use of the Box-Cox linearity<!-- XREF: EDA section 3.3, Graphical Techniques: Alphabetic, Box-Cox Linearity Plot; source handbook/eda/section3/boxcoxli.htm --> plot. The $\alpha$ value on the $x$ axis corresponding to the maximum correlation value on the $y$ axis indicates the power transformation that yields the most linear fit.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-pmd-624-boxcox
#| fig-cap: "Box-Cox linearity plot for ln(field defect size) versus a power-transformed lab defect size"
box_cox_transform <- function(x, alpha) {
  if (alpha == 0) log(x) else (x^alpha - 1) / alpha
}

boxcox_grid <- tibble(alpha = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 101)) |>
  filter(alpha != 0) |>
  mutate(
    correlation = map_dbl(alpha, ~ {
      tx <- box_cox_transform(berger$lab, .x)
      sqrt(summary(lm(log(berger$field) ~ tx))$r.squared)
    })
  )

ggplot(boxcox_grid, aes(alpha, correlation)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Alpha", y = "Correlation") +
  theme_light()
```

This plot indicates that a value of -0.1 achieves the most linear fit.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
boxcox_grid |> slice_max(correlation, n = 1)
```

In practice, for ease of interpretation, we often prefer to use a common transformation, such as the ln or square root, rather than the value that yields the mathematical maximum. However, the Box-Cox linearity plot still indicates whether our choice is a reasonable one. That is, we might sacrifice a small amount of linearity in the fit to have a simpler model.

In this case, a value of 0.0 would indicate a ln transformation. Although the optimal value from the plot is -0.1, the plot indicates that any value between -0.2 and 0.2 will yield fairly similar results. For that reason, we choose to stick with the common ln transformation.

[**ln-ln Fit**]{#sec-pmd-624-loglog-fit}

Based on the above plots, we choose to fit a ln-ln model.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
outt <- lm(log(field) ~ log(lab), data = berger)
loft <- lm(log(field) ~ factor(lab), data = berger)

summary(outt)
anova(outt, loft)
```

Note that although the residual standard deviation is significantly lower than it was for the original fit, we cannot compare them directly since the fits were performed on different scales.

[**Plot of Predicted Values**]{#sec-pmd-624-predicted}

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-pmd-624-overlay
#| fig-cap: "Transformed Alaska pipeline data overlaid with the fitted ln-ln model"
berger <- berger |> mutate(log_field = log(field), log_lab = log(lab), residualt = resid(outt), fittedt = fitted(outt))

ggplot(berger, aes(log_lab, log_field)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = fittedt), color = "firebrick") +
  labs(x = "ln(Lab Defect Size)", y = "ln(Field Defect Size)") +
  theme_light()
```

The plot of the predicted values with the transformed data indicates a good fit. In addition, the variability of the data across the horizontal range of the plot seems relatively constant.

[**6-Plot of Fit**]{#sec-pmd-624-6plot}

Since we transformed the data, we need to check that all of the regression assumptions are now valid.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| warning: false
#| label: fig-pmd-624-6plot
#| fig-cap: "6-plot for the ln-ln fit"
six_plot <- function(x, y, residual, fitted, xlab, ylab) {
  d <- tibble(x = x, y = y, residual = residual, fitted = fitted) |>
    mutate(lag_residual = lag(residual))

  p1 <- ggplot(d, aes(x, y)) +
    geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
    geom_line(aes(y = fitted), color = "firebrick") +
    labs(x = xlab, y = ylab, title = "Data with Fit") +
    theme_light()

  p2 <- ggplot(d, aes(x, residual)) +
    geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
    labs(x = xlab, y = "Residual", title = "Residuals vs Predictor") +
    theme_light()

  p3 <- ggplot(d, aes(fitted, residual)) +
    geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
    labs(x = "Predicted", y = "Residual", title = "Residuals vs Predicted") +
    theme_light()

  p4 <- ggplot(d, aes(lag_residual, residual)) +
    geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
    labs(x = "Residual[i-1]", y = "Residual[i]", title = "Lag Plot") +
    theme_light()

  p5 <- ggplot(d, aes(residual)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 15, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6, color = "white") +
    labs(x = "Residual", y = "Count", title = "Histogram") +
    theme_light()

  p6 <- ggplot(d, aes(sample = residual)) +
    stat_qq(color = "steelblue") +
    stat_qq_line(color = "firebrick") +
    labs(x = "Theoretical Quantiles", y = "Residual", title = "Normal Probability Plot") +
    theme_light()

  (p1 + p2 + p3) / (p4 + p5 + p6)
}

six_plot(berger$log_lab, berger$log_field, berger$residualt, berger$fittedt, "ln(Lab Defect Size)", "ln(Field Defect Size)")
```

The 6-plot of the residuals indicates that all of the regression assumptions are now satisfied.

[**Plot of Residuals**]{#sec-pmd-624-residuals}

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-pmd-624-residuals
#| fig-cap: "Residuals from the ln-ln fit versus ln(lab defect size)"
ggplot(berger, aes(log_lab, residualt)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "ln(Lab Defect Size)", y = "Residuals") +
  theme_light()
```

In order to see more detail, we generate a full-size plot of the residuals versus the predictor variable, as shown above. This plot suggests that the assumption of homogeneous variances is now met.
